This is a 40-inning sample in active play, so the read reflects early-season feel without the depth of conviction that comes with volume.

828685_hitter.text: Taitn Gray is an 18-year-old first baseman who walks as much as he hits — 31 free passes against 22% strikeouts in 192 A-ball PA gives him a .406 OBP that sits in the 90th percentile of his peer pool. The plate discipline is the real story here; his MLB-equivalent BB% translates to 10.5%, above the 8.5% league average, and that approach grade is the loudest tool on the card. Power is present (.188 ISO, .474 SLG at A-ball), but the MLB equivalent ISO of .132 lands below average, so the bat-to-ball and walk rate need to carry him while he adds strength. ValuCast projects a bench/platoon outcome as the most likely landing spot — ceiling of a low-end everyday regular, floor of a reserve — with two to three years until he gets there, and he's cooled one spot in ValuCast's rankings over the last three days.

829033_hitter.text: Elian Peña is an 18-year-old left-handed hitter showing disciplined plate recognition but struggling to generate impact; he's walking at 16.2% (87th percentile) while striking out at 19.7%, but his power grade is stalled at 35 with just .094 ISO. The core tension is that elite approach skills are masking a bat that hasn't yet shown the ability to do damage—his .752 OPS ranks only 55th among comparable hitters. Over 290 plate appearances in A-ball, the sample is fresh and clear, but still thin for a full skill assessment at this age.

829037_hitter.text: Kevin Alvarez, 18, is a young left-handed outfielder whose contact profile is deteriorating into strikeout trouble while his power remains modest for developmental purposes. At A-ball, he's struck out in 17.6% of his plate appearances but projects to 22.9% K% at the MLB level, while his .167 ISO barely exceeds organizational average; his .322 OBP lags the 31st percentile, a direct result of a 6.9% walk rate that will not sustain him through the minors. ValuCast's projection pegs him for organizational depth—with 77% probability of a bench or platoon role—reflecting mixed hit and approach grades (55 and 40, respectively) on a modest three-year arc. The 233 PA sample is fresh and clean, but early strikeout rate at this age is a legitimate red flag without offsetting plate discipline or raw power.

829052_hitter.text: Breyson Guedez is a young left-handed hitter working through strikeout noise at the A level, flashing contact ability (.282 avg, 83rd percentile) but generating minimal power (.119 ISO, 31st percentile) and very little leverage on base (6.6% BB rate, 8th percentile). At 18 with only 272 plate appearances, the strikeout rate (29%) sits just above major-league average in the translation, a concerning baseline for someone still learning pitch recognition. The hit tool is real, but without secondary skills or early power development, the path to impact is narrow.

829058_hitter.text: Gabriel Davalillo is an 18-year-old third baseman showing mixed bat discipline and pop: he's posting .267/.348/.410 with an 11% walk rate and .143 ISO over 227 A-ball plate appearances, though both his strikeout rate (25.6%) and isolated power rank near the middle of the minor-league field. The real concern is that his average and slugging power lag below the tools expected at the position—his .267 AVG is strong for his age, but ISO in the 47th percentile signals he hasn't yet connected the bat to game power. The sample is current and meaningful, but at 18 with moderate command and modest thump so far, this looks like a years-away organizational depth profile rather than a near-term contributor.

829210_hitter.text: Ty Harvey is a 19-year-old catcher showing early discipline at the plate—19% BB% on a 58 PA sample—but swinging and missing at a concerning clip (24.1% K%). His .107 ISO translates to below-average raw power for a catcher, and the strikeout rate (24.1%), even accounting for youth, sits above league average in the MLB equivalent read. The sample is small and fresh, so expect volatility as he faces stiffer velocity and sequencing.

829854_hitter.text: Luis Arana is an 18-year-old A-level shortstop who commands the strike zone exceptionally—posting 19.2% BB% over 78 PA—but whose overall bat lacks impact, evidenced by a modest .127 ISO and a .460 SLG despite the strong .462 OBP. The approach grade is elite relative to his peer group; the hit tool is solid; but power and overall impact are well below average, and that power ceiling is the central constraint. At 78 plate appearances in a current season sample, confidence in the profile is limited, though the plate discipline suggests a repeatable skill.

830239_hitter.text: Aaron Walton is a power-dominant hitter with the bat speed to impact games but a swing-and-miss problem that could limit his floor. His .513 SLG and .24 ISO rank in the 91st percentile at his level, but he's striking out in 28.4% of his at-bats—well above league average even in translation. The 285 PA sample is clean and current, though MLB-equivalent projection shows his strikeout rate holding near 30%, which will compress his offensive value if it persists at the majors.

830336_pitcher.text: Mason Peters is a pure bat-missing lefty arm operating at elite efficiency levels on a brief but dominant A-ball sample. He's striking out 12.7 per 9 innings while walking just 1.6, putting him in the 99th percentile for both strikeout rate and K-BB% among the ValuCast pitcher pool. The hard flaw: this is 44.7 innings on A-ball, and when translated to MLB-equivalent rates his walk rate jumps to 2.7 per 9 while strikeouts fall to 8.5—a much tighter margin that raises questions about whether the command grades hold at higher competition. ValuCast is ranking him upward, but the sample is small and the level is low, so confidence in any ceiling projection remains guarded.

830402_pitcher.text: Kendry Chourio is an 18-year-old command artist who doesn't miss bats — and at A/A+, that's a profile worth understanding clearly before you fall in love with the ERA. The 2.5 ERA and 0.9 WHIP are real; his BB/9 of 1.7 and WHIP sit at the 98th and 97th percentiles respectively against his pitcher pool, and a K-BB% of 20% shows he's not walking people into trouble. The problem is the strikeout rate — 8.9 K/9 in A-ball translates to a projected 7.2 at the MLB level, below the 8.6 average, and the miss grade here is a 35 — so the question isn't whether his command is special, it's whether there's enough swing-and-miss to survive as he climbs. ValuCast projects a useful MLB arm as the most likely outcome, with the ceiling a depth arm and a multi-inning floor, and he's ticking up slightly in ValuCast's rankings over the last three days — but the outcome here lives or dies on whether the strikeout tool develops.

832562_pitcher.text: Dylan Brown is a left-handed pitcher operating as a bat-missing arm at A+, with a 13.2 K/9 that ranks 93rd percentile among the ValuCast pitcher pool and a K-BB% of 26.6% (97th percentile) that signals elite strikeout-to-walk separation. The main drag is run prevention—his 4.05 ERA and 1.38 WHIP (both around 61st percentile) show balls are finding play despite the impressive strikeout rate, a gap the translation model flags at higher uncertainty. The projection sees a multi-inning or setup arm ceiling over two to three years, though this is a modest 33.3 IP current sample with no stale-date risk.

834962_hitter.text: Anthony DePino is a power-over-hit hitter still learning the zone at 23, showing the thump—.504 SLG, .229 ISO at 89th percentile—but swinging through enough pitches (22.9% K) to keep him from running away with offensive impact. His walk rate sits at a respectable 13.4%, and the .886 OPS reflects a bat with real juice, though the strikeout volume tempers the consistency. The main risk is whether he can stay in the lineup without more contact; he projects as organizational depth with a bench-or-platoon ceiling (85% probability), needing to trim strikeouts and tighten his approach to climb higher. This is a fresh 157-PA sample, so the power is real but the hit tool remains unsettled enough to watch closely.

834978_pitcher.text: Danny Thompson Jr. is a right-handed pitcher showing plus strikeout stuff paired with walk management that trails his miss rate—a profile built on swing-and-miss with control that lags behind the swing-and-miss. In his A+ sample (47.3 IP), he struck out 12.93 per 9 while walking 4.56 per 9, a K-BB% of 21.9% that ranks 91st percentile among ValuCast's pitcher pool. The core risk is whether he can sustain that strikeout rate as competition tightens; his current AA sample is only 9 IP, making any read here thin and provisional. Floor is a depth arm, with modest probability of reaching useful depth relief value in the next one to two years.
